text: Connecting to Azure SQL Database follows the exact same pattern Lesson 7 already taught, start to finish. Manage, Linked services, New, search for the connector, and configure it — server name, database name, and an authentication type: SQL authentication, Microsoft Entra ID, or a managed identity.
Because Data Factory and Azure SQL Database both live in Azure's own cloud, the default Azure Integration Runtime reaches it directly, with no extra infrastructure decision required at all.
Searching for and configuring the SQL Server connector looks almost completely identical — same gallery, same search box, same general shape of form.

But look closely at Connect via integration runtime. This is where the real difference actually lives. If your SQL Server instance sits inside an on-premises network, or any private network the Azure Integration Runtime simply can't reach, you need a self-hosted integration runtime instead — Chapter 7's topic — installed on a machine that genuinely can reach it.

Azure SQL reaches directly, cloud to cloud, no extra setup. On-premises SQL Server needs that self-hosted bridge instead, installed on your own network, accepting requests from the cloud and relaying them securely, without ever exposing that server to the public internet.

Every lab from here forward touching AdventureWorks or Northwind through Data Factory depends on exactly this piece being installed and online. Next: datasets, the other half of every connection — which specific data, inside that connection, you actually mean.
